title: CSQ Unit 7 · Make Your Own Game (3-5)

items.q: A drawing of each screen of a game, made before building, is a…
choices: packet
cipher
storyboard
sensor

items.q: The first step of making a game for someone is…
choices: add music first
build it as fast as you can
pick a color for the title
decide who it is for and plan

items.q: Why ask "who is this game for?" before building?
choices: because the Builder asks
so the game fits the player's needs
to make it longer
to skip testing

items.q: In your pair, the tester/note-taker should…
choices: type every message to the Builder
decide everything without asking
do nothing until it is done
play the game and write what happened

items.q: Splitting your game into "start screen", "playing" and "winning" is…
choices: looping
encryption
debugging
decomposition

items.q: After every change to your game you should…
choices: send two more messages
play it to test the change
close the Builder
change the title

items.q: The Builder made the rocket fly down instead of up. Which message is best?
choices: "it is wrong"
"I expected the rocket to fly up when I tap; it flies down. Please fix."
"make it cool"
"add more rockets and a dog"

items.q: Why send one change per message?
choices: so you can test each change and see what fixed what
because messages have to be short
to use up more of the messages
so the Builder gets a rest between them
your favorite colors
the names of your friends
the game's price
things to try and what should happen
what they noticed while playing your game
a bug the Builder put in the game
the score at the end of the game
a kind of loop in the game

items.q: Why get feedback from different people?
choices: one person's opinion is always enough
different players notice different things
it is faster than testing yourself
so nobody has to play it twice

items.q: Two testers said level 2 is confusing. What next?
choices: ignore them, they played wrong
delete the game
change level 2 and test again
add more levels

items.q: While a tester plays, the maker should…
choices: tell them every move to make
play the game instead of them
leave the room until they finish
watch where they get stuck, without helping

items.q: Explaining why you chose a timer in your game is…
choices: debugging the timer
encrypting the timer
describing a design choice
sorting the game's parts

items.q: A good 60-second demo tells the audience…
choices: who it is for and one choice you made and why
your passphrase and your login
every bug the game ever had
nothing, you just play in silence
list every line of code in the game
be kept secret from the players
be longer than the game itself
tell a new player what to do in a few lines
your birthday and your age
your passphrase, in case it is needed
people, art and ideas you used
nothing at all, it is your game
